title: A handover sheet on the bus
stem: You are an F2 doctor in general surgery. On the bus home, you find a printed surgical handover sheet on the seat next to you. It lists patients' names, dates of birth and diagnoses from your hospital.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Keep it safe and return it for confidential disposal.
options.detailed: The sheet contains confidential information. Keeping it safe and disposing of it through the hospital's confidential waste protects the patients.

options.text: Leave it on the bus, as it isn't yours.
options.detailed: It isn't yours, but leaving it means others could read it.

options.text: Put it in a bin at the bus stop.
options.detailed: This gets rid of it, but a public bin isn't secure, and others could find and read it.

options.text: Report it as an information governance incident.
options.brief: The trust needs to know about the breach.
options.detailed: A lost handover sheet is a data breach. Reporting it lets the trust assess the risk and learn from it.

options.text: Take a photo of it to show the surgical team, then throw it away.
options.brief: Creates another copy of confidential information.
options.detailed: Photographing it creates a second copy of patients' confidential details on your personal phone, which adds to the breach rather than containing it.

options.text: Read it to find out whose it is.
options.detailed: This seems sensible, but you don't need to read patient details to report it.

options.text: Let the surgical team know a sheet was found.
options.brief: Helps them check their handover practice.
options.detailed: The team may not know a sheet was lost. Telling them helps prevent it happening again.
Household recycling isn't confidential disposal, and the sheet could still be read by others before it is destroyed.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you protect confidential information you find, and report the breach.
explanation.keyDetails: The sheet contains identifiable information. It was left in public. It belongs to your hospital.
explanation.reasoning: [A] secures it, [D] reports the breach, and [G] helps prevent another. The distractors leave it exposed ([B], [C], [H]), add to the breach ([E]), or read it unnecessarily ([F]).
explanation.competing: [F] may seem reasonable, but you don't need to read the details to report it.

references.title: Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information
references.note: Protecting patients' information and reporting breaches.
